titleStmt.title: Telegram From the Department of State to the Embassy in Uruguay

div.head: 447. Telegram From the Department of State to the Embassy in Uruguay
div.p: 2. Summary: Foreign Minister Maeso had no real agenda for his October 4 bilateral with Assistant Secretary Motley, but his message was clear: You’ll miss us when we’re gone. Maeso noted the warmth of our bilateral relations in recent years but cautioned that the US could expect relations to cool in the future, regardless of who wins the election. Maeso warned that Cuba will help revivify the left in Uruguay and that this will contribute to more strident criticism of U.S. policy in Central America, among other things. He noted that the Blanco Party is already moving to the left under the leadership of Wilson Ferreira’s son, Juan Raul. According to Maeso, the natural custodians of democracy in Uruguay are the armed forces, and he urged that the US enhance relations with them. Maeso characterized negotiations with the IMF as going badly and asked the US to “talk to the IMF” on Uruguay’s behalf. As he said good-bye, Maeso invited the USG to send observers to the November elections.

3. On October 4, 1984 Assistant Secretary Motley, accompanied by the desk officer, met with Foreign Minister Maeso, Uruguayan UN Ambassador Juan Carlos Blanco and MFA Foreign Policy Director Alvaro Alvarez. The Foreign Minister initiated the conversation by noting that this would be his last UNGA and then commented on the state of U.S.-Uruguayan relations. In the hour long conversation that followed, most of which was guided by a few questions from Ambassador Motley, Maeso made the
following points:

Our bilateral relations will cool: Maeso predicted that with the help of conservative former President Pacheco, the Colorados will win in November. No matter who wins, however, the US should expect cooler relations with Uruguay as the country repudiates the current regime and looks toward Europe for support. Maeso urged the US to be patient. He believes that institutional and political ties forged between our countries in recent years are now too strong to be entirely undone or forgotten.

Relations with Brazil will cool: Maeso expects the next government to tilt towards Argentina. He asserted, however, that his government’s efforts to strengthen ties with Brazil would endure, in part because Brazil would not permit otherwise.

The left will gain ground in Uruguay: Maeso warned that after the elections relations are likely to be restored with Cuba, which will cause problems for Uruguay and the U.S. alike. Cuba will abet the left in its efforts to extend its influence internally. In foreign policy this will lead to more strident criticism of U.S. policy in Central America among other things. According to Maeso, there are 1,500 Uruguayans with Tupamaro connections in Cuba. GOU intelligence services indicate that for the last eight months former Uruguayan guerrillas and sympathizers have been drifting back towards home. Maeso is particularly concerned that the left will be able to play a spoiler role in the Uruguayan Parliament, where he does not expect moderates to control more than 40 of the votes even if the Colorados win. (The remaining 60 would presumably be composed of leftists drawn primarily from the majority faction of the Blanco Party and the leftist coalition Frente Amplio.)

Maintain ties with the military: The Foreign Minister urged that the U.S. enhance relations with the armed forces, which he characterized as perhaps not up to the job of governing but not corrupt and certainly not tainted with human rights abuses as in Argentina. He does not believe that the Uruguayan military will be infiltrated by the left as has happened elsewhere in Latin America because in Uruguay the armed forces are “the natural custodians of democracy.” Six months after the inauguration, Maeso predicted, people will longingly remember the tranquility afforded by the current government.

Assistant Secretary Motley noted that he and Ambassador Aranda shared the view that we should make an effort to
shore up the confidence of Uruguay’s military and demonstrate that there are rewards in returning the country to its democratic traditions. The Foreign Minister agreed and praised Ambassador Aranda for his warmth and the exceptional way he has integrated himself into the Uruguayan scene.

We need help from our friends: In response to queries about the IMF negotiation, Maeso noted that negotiations are going badly. Despite sound economic policies and a responsible posture on regional debt, Uruguay now finds itself alone—“like Adam without Eve”—as it tries to negotiate with the IMF. Vegh is demoralized and angered by the IMF’s refusal to consider less tangible, but equally important, social and political factors in negotiating a new stand-by agreement. A failure to gain IMF approval will undermine moderates in the elections and increase anti-American feeling, the Foreign Minister warned. He then asked for the U.S. to “talk to the IMF” on Uruguay’s behalf.

Ambassador Motley noted that the IMF staff is stretched thin but is gradually coming to understand the importance of the socio-political factors to which Maeso referred. For that reason it is essential that the GOU continues its talks with the fund, as difficult and frustrating as this may be. As for talking to the fund, Motley pointed out that contrary to common belief, we do not own it and indeed must be very circumspect in our dealings with its officials. The most anyone could do would be to address the Uruguayan case at the margins and in the context of broader concerns. This we could and would do.

4. As the meeting closed Maeso said he would not attend the Panamanian inauguration on his way home but would visit Costa Rica instead. He also extended an invitation for the USG to send observers for the elections in November. Uruguay, he noted pointedly, has a tradition of welcoming serious observers who do not come with preconceived notions.

note.p: Source: Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D840642–1032. Confidential. Immediate. Drafted by Kinney; cleared by Kilday and ARA/SC; approved by Motley.

In telegram 4810 from Montevideo, August 14, Aranda wrote for Motley: “I agree that, despite the difficulties, the political transition in Uruguay is going well and that our policy of evenhandedness and quiet support for the return to democracy is paying off. I also agree with your feeling about perceptions perhaps not reflecting this reality in Washington, but disagree that our efforts are not widely appreciated in Uruguay. They are understood and appreciated by most Uruguayans, including the PLP faction (Ferreira) of the Blanco Party, whose leaders continue to regard us as effective interlocutors with Uruguayan authorities.” (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, N840009–0604) In telegram 244788 to Montevideo, August 18, the Department reported on Abrams’ August 16 meeting with Ravenna, who “began by emphasizing the correctness and effectiveness of US ‘quiet diplomacy’ over the past several years. In his view, this had played a decisive role in stimulating favorable trends toward the restoration of democratically elected civilian leaders in Uruguay; he added that a strident, public posture on the part of outsiders could well have produced the opposite effect. Thus, Ravenna said, virtually all segments of the political spectrum were in agreement about the need for the upcoming transition to popularly elected civilian leadership after the November 25 elections.” (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D840528–0469)

In an October 13 memorandum to Reagan, McFarlane noted that Betancur had written to Reagan urging him “to support democracy in Uruguay and to intercede on behalf of the detained opposition leader, Wilson Ferreira.” McFarlane called Ferreira’s detention “the major flaw in an otherwise positive picture” regarding the restoration of Uruguayan democracy. Reagan agreed to send an October 17 letter to Betancur affirming U.S. support for the democratic transition in Uruguay and noting, among other things, his administration’s “special effort” to “convey privately to Uruguayan officials” U.S. concerns about Ferreira’s June arrest. “We are hopeful,” Reagan wrote, “that our continuing representations will help to assure just and humane treatment for Dr. Ferreira.” (Reagan Library, NSC Records, Latin American Affairs Directorate, Country File, Colombia (10/10/1984–11/30/1984))

In telegram 338277 to Montevideo, November 19, 1983, the Department reported on Motley’s November 18, 1983 meeting with Maeso during which Maeso asked for the U.S. to help convince Brazil to grant Uruguay more favorable trading status. (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D830701–0744)

In telegram 7196 from Montevideo, November 26, 1984, the Embassy reported on Uruguay’s national elections, writing “Sanguinetti and the Colorados win.” (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D840753–0535) Alan Riding wrote in the New York Times: “In the last 11 years, while thousands of Uruguayans were jailed and tens of thousands more were forced into exile, Julio María Sanguinetti avoided a confrontation with the military regime, convinced that it could be coaxed—but never forced—out of office. Mr. Sanguinetti’s election Sunday in Uruguay’s first presidential elections since 1971 provided the vindication of this strategy: two outspoken political leaders were banned as candidates, but the dictatorship should end on March 1.” (Alan Riding, “Peacemaker For Uruguay: Julio María Sanguinetti,” New York Times, November 27, 1984, p. A10) In telegram 350439 to Montevideo, November 28, 1984, the Department forward the text of Reagan’s congratulatory message to Sanguinetti, in which Reagan noted, “The American people and I have looked forward to the day when Uruguay could return to its democratic traditions” and, “We look forward to enhanced cooperation with Uruguay and its people as we strive to address the great issues facing our nations and the hemisphere.” (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D840758–0960)
